text: Non-Destructive Testing RUS Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) is a NDE method that offers a powerful tool for determining the moduli of AM metals. The material science tetrahedron, illustrated in Figure 17(a), aptly demonstrates the intricate relationships between the various aspects of metal behavior. Specifically, the structure and part properties are shaped by the fabrication process, which in turn affects the overall performance of the part. Each of these aspects can be characterized to understand their interdependencies. Similarly, the capabilities of RUS can be represented by a tetrahedron, as shown in Figure 17(b). Here, a specific geometry is associated with a density that is directly influenced by the defects introduced during fabrication and any unresolved issues resulting from post-processing. This, in turn, impacts the material properties, which directly influence the elastic moduli and, by extension, the mechanical behavior. RUS, combined with finite element analysis, can be employed to calculate these moduli. In FY24, a series of RUS screenings were conducted to investigate the heterogeneity of fabricated 316H samples at various processing parameters, providing valuable insights into the material's behavior. Figure 16: The (a) material science tetrahedron, and (b) RUS tetrahedron. In RUS, mechanical resonances are measured using transducers that vibrate the part, generating a spectrum of amplitude peaks at distinct frequencies, as illustrated in Figure 18. The operator inputs the part's geometry and mass into a computational model, which is then processed through a generic algorithm. This algorithm iteratively calculates the resonance frequencies, making adjustments and eliminating errors until the calculated frequencies converge with the measured frequencies. By leveraging this approach, RUS enables the accurate determination of a material's elastic moduli, providing valuable insights into its mechanical properties. Figure 17: RUS frequency scan and process algorithm. The longitudinal and shear moduli obtained from the RUS scans are utilized to calculate the bulk and Young's moduli, employing Equations 2 and 3. The results of these calculations are presented in Figure 19, showcasing the moduli values for each distinct parameter within the operating window established during the initial development study. Notably, all samples underwent heat treatment at 650°C for 24 hours. A thorough examination of the results reveals that the moduli are indeed sensitive to the processing parameters, with outliers evident at both extremes (high and low) of the operating window. This suggests that the processing conditions have a significant impact on the material's elastic properties, underscoring the importance of optimizing these parameters to achieve desired material behavior. Upon examining the results, general trends emerge that correlate with the corresponding processing parameters. A key finding from this study is that the Young's modulus stands out as the most reliable predictor of build quality. Although it was not possible to directly quantify the amount of porosity present in the samples during this investigation, distinct trends are apparent, suggesting that the elastic moduli can be used to quickly identify patterns and correlations.
